content: The Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) and the WHO Pocket Book of Hospital Care for Children provide foundational guidance for managing severe acute malnutrition in children. However, the guideline group noted that specific guidelines for infants under six months of age with severe acute malnutrition have not been previously developed. This includes practices such as establishing effective exclusive breastfeeding by the mother or caregiver and assessing the physical and mental health of mothers. The group emphasized that these recommendations represent essential principles of care, which may not be easily evaluated through randomized controlled trials. They concluded that implementing these practices, even in the absence of clinical or cost data, would likely benefit infants with severe acute malnutrition without significant risk of harm. The guideline group identified several priority research areas for infants under six months of age with severe acute malnutrition. These include determining the predictive value of population-derived thresholds for weight-for-height, mid-upper arm circumference, and reduced growth velocity (weight-for-age), with or without edema, in identifying infants at high risk of mortality. They also highlighted the need to evaluate the feasibility of these assessments. Additionally, the group sought to identify the most effective and safest therapeutic feeding approaches, including various food formulations alongside breastfeeding, for this age group. Another critical area of interest is understanding how to most effectively re-establish breastfeeding among infants with low weight-for-height or poor weight gain. Further research questions include whether infants under six months of age with a weight-for-length Z-score below -3 also exhibit reduced growth velocity and whether this varies by epidemiological setting, such as in African, South Asian, or Southeast Asian regions. The feasibility and accuracy of using weight-for-height, mid-upper arm circumference, and reduced growth velocity (with or without edema) to identify infants requiring therapeutic management were also considered. The group also sought to determine the criteria that best identify metabolic abnormalities or adaptations associated with severe acute malnutrition in older children and their relevance to younger infants. The effectiveness, tolerance, and safety of ready-to-use therapeutic food as an adjunct to breastfeeding in infants under six months of age with severe acute malnutrition were also highlighted as a research priority. This includes specific subgroups, such as those with edema, those aged four to six months, and those with underlying conditions like HIV. The group also raised questions about the recommended folic acid supplementation for this population and whether adjustments in drug dosages or drug selection are necessary when managing infants with severe acute malnutrition. Additionally, they questioned whether the efficacy of vitamin A supplementation differs between infants under six months of age with severe acute malnutrition and those aged one to five months without severe acute malnutrition. The WHO has developed a centralized platform to compile and share information on nutrition-related public health practices worldwide. This platform aims to provide examples of how guidelines are being translated into actionable nutrition interventions by sharing programmatic details, country-specific adaptations, and lessons learned. The current guideline, along with other updated child health guidelines, will serve as the basis for revising the WHO manual and training courses on managing severe malnutrition. Countries have requested this updated guidance to revise their national protocols and improve their capacity to manage severe malnutrition effectively. The guideline development process followed WHO's evidence-informed procedures, as outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. This involved identifying priority questions and outcomes, commissioning systematic reviews to retrieve relevant evidence, and assessing the quality of evidence using the GRADE approach. Evidence from randomized controlled trials was generally rated as high quality, while evidence from observational studies was rated as low quality. Factors such as study limitations, consistency, directness, imprecision, and reporting bias were considered when adjusting these initial ratings. The findings were synthesized into GRADE tables for critical outcomes, while data for important but non-critical outcomes were summarized narratively. Draft recommendations were prepared by WHO staff and reviewed by the Nutrition Guidance Advisory Group (NUGAG), which considered the desirable and undesirable effects of interventions, the quality of evidence, values and preferences in different settings, and cost implications. Consensus was defined as agreement by a simple majority of guideline group members. A public call for comments on the final draft guideline was issued, and feedback was received from 20 stakeholders and external experts. WHO staff finalized the guideline and submitted it for clearance before publication. To manage conflicts of interest, all experts participating in WHO meetings were required to declare any relevant interests before their participation. Declarations of interest were reviewed by the responsible technical officer and relevant departments before finalizing the group composition. Participants also verbally declared potential conflicts of interest at the beginning of each meeting. The procedures for managing conflicts of interest strictly adhered to WHO guidelines.
